issues.legal_issue: A one-off acquisition and resale of land constitutes an adventure in the nature of trade when the transaction’s purpose and conduct, considered together, show an organised profit-making scheme.
material_facts: The taxpayer agreed to acquire a large estate for a price far beyond his financial resources and paid an advance, with the conveyance permitted to be made to him or his nominees.
The taxpayer divided the estate into 23 plots and arranged purchasers for 22 plots before conveyance; those plots were conveyed to the purchasers and the remaining plot was conveyed to the taxpayer.
The taxpayer lacked the resources to cultivate the estate himself, and the arrangement and subdivision showed planning and organisation directed to resale.
issues.conclusion: The transactions were an adventure in the nature of trade, carried out as part of a profit-making scheme, and the resulting profit was taxable.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade depends on the total impression and effect of all relevant facts and circumstances; no single abstract test or formula governs. Relevant considerations include the transaction’s relation to the taxpayer’s ordinary business, the nature and scale of the acquisition, the taxpayer’s intention, subsequent dealings, organisation, and manner of disposal. The Court applied section 34(1)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, in the assessment context and relied on California Copper Syndicate v. Harris, Martin v. Lowry, Rutledge v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, Leeming v. Jones, Saroj Kumar Mazumdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Raja J. Rameshwar Rao v. Commissioner of Income-tax.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and land_acquired_for_profit_resale and land_divided_into_plots and purchasers_arranged_for_most_plots and taxpayer_lacked_means_to_cultivate_land

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The taxpayer was involved in an income-tax assessment concerning gains from a transaction.
predicates.land_acquired_for_profit_resale: The taxpayer acquired land under an arrangement indicating an intention to resell it for profit.
predicates.land_divided_into_plots: The taxpayer divided the acquired land into separate plots.
predicates.purchasers_arranged_for_most_plots: The taxpayer arranged purchasers for most of the plots before conveyance.
predicates.taxpayer_lacked_means_to_cultivate_land: The taxpayer lacked the means to cultivate the land personally.

issues.definition: When a taxpayer in an income-tax assessment acquires land for profitable resale, divides it into plots, arranges purchasers for most plots, and lacks means to cultivate it, the transaction is treated as an adventure in the nature of trade.

issues.legal_issue: Profit from a trading adventure may be computed for an accounting year by including the value of land retained as stock-in-trade, even though that land has not yet been sold.
material_facts: The taxpayer sold 22 plots during the accounting period and retained the remaining plot, which was conveyed to him.
The tax officer treated the retained plot as stock-in-trade, estimated its value, and included that value with the sale proceeds when computing the transaction’s profit.
The taxpayer argued that profit could not be ascertained until the retained plot was sold.
issues.conclusion: The profit was correctly estimated by treating the retained land as stock-in-trade and valuing it according to normal accountancy practice; the profit did not have to await the later sale of the retained plot.
issues.legal_principle: For income-tax assessment, each year is a self-contained unit, and profits from a trading adventure must be computed under the Act using true accountancy practice. Although the Income-tax Act, 1922, contains no express provision specifying stock valuation, stock-in-trade is ordinarily taken into account by valuing it at the beginning and end of the accounting period. The Court relied on Whimster & Co. v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Cock, Russell & Co. Ltd., and Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras v. A. Krishnaswami Mudaliar & Ors.; it also noted that ordinary commercial accounting principles apply so far as they do not conflict with an express statutory provision.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and transaction_is_a_trading_adventure and land_retained_at_accounting_period_end and retained_land_treated_as_stock_in_trade

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The taxpayer’s profits were being computed in an income-tax assessment.
predicates.transaction_is_a_trading_adventure: The taxpayer’s transaction was treated as a trading adventure.
predicates.land_retained_at_accounting_period_end: The taxpayer retained land at the end of the accounting period without having sold it.
predicates.retained_land_treated_as_stock_in_trade: The tax officer treated the retained land as stock-in-trade and assigned it a value.

issues.definition: If an income-tax assessment concerns a trading adventure in which land remains unsold at the end of the accounting period and is treated as stock-in-trade, its value may be included in computing that year’s profit.
